lessons.title: Why version control matters
lessons.summary: Track your project as snapshots rather than losing work in folders named final-v7. A commit records a version of a tracked tree with a message and parent history.

lab.prompt: Confirm that Git is installed by requesting its version.
lab.hint: Run the version flag on git.

concepts.definition: A project directory containing Git metadata and a history of tracked snapshots.
A recorded snapshot of tracked content, its message, parent(s), and metadata.
The actual checked-out files you edit before staging or committing.

scenario.question: You want to experiment without losing yesterday’s working code. What should you use?
scenario.explanation: Branches let experiments diverge without rewriting a stable line of work.

lessons.tip: A commit is not a backup of every untracked file; only content that was added to the history is retained.
lessons.objective: Explain repository and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Repository: A project directory containing Git metadata and a history of tracked snapshots.
Commit: A recorded snapshot of tracked content, its message, parent(s), and metadata.
Working tree: The actual checked-out files you edit before staging or committing.
lessons.questStory: Mission 01: Your team needs you to apply why version control matters safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Initialize and inspect
lessons.summary: A repository starts with git init. Status is your dashboard: it distinguishes tracked, changed, staged, and untracked files.

lab.prompt: Initialize a repository in an empty practice directory.
lab.hint: The command ends in init.

concepts.definition: Creates Git metadata in the current directory; it does not publish anything online.
Reports branch, staged changes, unstaged changes, and untracked files.
A file Git sees but has never been added for tracking.

scenario.question: After creating notes.md, git status calls it untracked. Why?
options: Git has not been told to track it
scenario.explanation: Files stay untracked until explicitly added, unless ignored.

lessons.tip: Run commands in a disposable folder; do not initialize inside an unrelated project.
lessons.objective: Explain git init and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: git init: Creates Git metadata in the current directory; it does not publish anything online.
git status: Reports branch, staged changes, unstaged changes, and untracked files.
Untracked file: A file Git sees but has never been added for tracking.
lessons.questStory: Mission 02: Your team needs you to apply initialize and inspect safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Stage and commit changes
lessons.summary: The index (staging area) lets you choose the exact version that goes into the next commit. Stage deliberately; commit with an informative message.
lessons.example:
git add README.md
git commit -m "Document setup"

lab.prompt: Stage only README.md, leaving other files untouched.
lab.hint: Use git add followed by the filename.

concepts.definition: The index: the proposed content of the next commit, separate from your working tree.
Copies the current version of selected paths into the index.
Records the staged snapshot as a new history entry.

scenario.question: You changed two files but only want to commit one. What do you do?
scenario.explanation: Staging a path limits what goes into the next commit.

lessons.tip: A commit records staged content, not automatically every last working-tree edit.
lessons.objective: Explain staging area and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Staging area: The index: the proposed content of the next commit, separate from your working tree.
git add: Copies the current version of selected paths into the index.
git commit: Records the staged snapshot as a new history entry.
lessons.questStory: Mission 03: Your team needs you to apply stage and commit changes safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Read history and diffs
lessons.summary: Read the past before rewriting it. git log shows commits, git diff compares changes; --staged shows what is queued for the next commit.

lab.prompt: Inspect staged changes before committing.
lab.hint: Use git diff with a long flag describing the index.

concepts.definition: Displays commit history and metadata, optionally condensed with --oneline.
Shows line-level differences; plain form normally compares working tree to index.
Makes git diff compare the staging area with the current HEAD commit.

scenario.question: Which command reviews what your next commit will contain?
scenario.explanation: Staged diff shows patch content rather than just filenames.

lessons.tip: Always review a diff before committing credentials or generated files.
lessons.objective: Explain git log and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: git log: Displays commit history and metadata, optionally condensed with --oneline.
git diff: Shows line-level differences; plain form normally compares working tree to index.
--staged: Makes git diff compare the staging area with the current HEAD commit.
lessons.questStory: Mission 04: Your team needs you to apply read history and diffs safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Branches, merges, and recovery
lessons.summary: Branches are pointers to commits. Create an isolated feature branch, merge reviewed changes, and prefer revert when undoing already-shared history.
lessons.example:
git switch -c feature/login
git switch main
git merge feature/login

lab.prompt: Create a new branch called feature/login and switch to it.
lab.hint: Use switch with -c and a feature branch name.

concepts.definition: A movable reference to a commit that gives a line of work a name.
Integrates another branch’s changes, possibly creating a merge commit.
Creates a new commit that inverses an earlier commit without deleting published history.

scenario.question: You must undo a bad commit already pulled by teammates. What is the safest default?
scenario.explanation: Revert preserves shared history and adds a compensating commit.

lessons.tip: Never casually force-push a shared branch; coordinate when history rewriting is truly necessary.
lessons.objective: Explain branch and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Branch: A movable reference to a commit that gives a line of work a name.
Merge: Integrates another branch’s changes, possibly creating a merge commit.
git revert: Creates a new commit that inverses an earlier commit without deleting published history.
lessons.questStory: Mission 05: Your team needs you to apply branches, merges, and recovery safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Remote repositories
lessons.summary: Git lives locally; GitHub hosts collaboration. A remote is a named URL, and push/pull exchange reachable commits and refs.
lessons.example:
git remote -v
git remote add origin https://github.com/USER/REPO.git

lab.prompt: List the remotes configured for your repository.
lab.hint: Show configured remotes verbosely.

concepts.definition: A named address for another Git repository, commonly origin.
Uploads local commits/refs to a remote when permissions and history allow.
Downloads remote refs and objects without automatically merging them.

scenario.question: You want new remote commits but not an automatic merge. Choose:
scenario.explanation: Fetch updates remote-tracking refs; pull additionally integrates.

lessons.tip: Never paste private access tokens into a remote URL stored in a public screenshot.
lessons.objective: Explain remote and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Remote: A named address for another Git repository, commonly origin.
git push: Uploads local commits/refs to a remote when permissions and history allow.
git fetch: Downloads remote refs and objects without automatically merging them.
lessons.questStory: Mission 06: Your team needs you to apply remote repositories safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Pull requests and reviews
lessons.summary: A pull request proposes changes from a head branch into a base branch. Use a clear description, review the diff, and wait for required checks.

lab.prompt: Publish your local feature branch and set its upstream.
lab.hint: Use git push with -u to remember the upstream.

concepts.definition: A discussion and review workflow for integrating branch changes.
The destination branch into which a PR proposes changes.
Human feedback, approval, or change requests on proposed code.

scenario.question: A check fails on your PR. What should you do before merging?
scenario.explanation: A failed required check can indicate broken tests or unsafe changes.

lessons.tip: Reviewers should understand what changed, why, and how it was tested.
lessons.objective: Explain pull request and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Pull request: A discussion and review workflow for integrating branch changes.
Base branch: The destination branch into which a PR proposes changes.
Review: Human feedback, approval, or change requests on proposed code.
lessons.questStory: Mission 07: Your team needs you to apply pull requests and reviews safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Forks, issues, and contributions
lessons.summary: Use issues to record scoped work and forks to propose changes when you do not have direct write access. Link a branch and PR to the issue.

lab.prompt: Inspect all local and remote-tracking branch names.
lab.hint: The branch command can include all references with -a.

concepts.definition: A separate repository derived from another repository, often used for contributions.
A tracked piece of work, bug report, or discussion item.
A conventional name for the original repository when your fork uses origin.

scenario.question: You cannot push to an open-source project. Which contribution path fits?
options: Download and edit the ZIP only
scenario.explanation: A fork enables collaboration without direct write access to the source repository.

lessons.tip: Keep PRs focused; one small issue per PR is easier to review.
lessons.objective: Explain fork and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Fork: A separate repository derived from another repository, often used for contributions.
Issue: A tracked piece of work, bug report, or discussion item.
Upstream remote: A conventional name for the original repository when your fork uses origin.
lessons.questStory: Mission 08: Your team needs you to apply forks, issues, and contributions safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Resolve merge conflicts
lessons.summary: A conflict occurs when Git cannot reconcile overlapping changes automatically. Inspect conflict markers, decide desired content, stage resolution, then finish the operation.

lab.prompt: Check files for whitespace errors and conflict-related formatting mistakes.
lab.hint: Use diff with the --check flag.

concepts.definition: Temporary <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> lines identifying competing edits.
Human-selected merged content staged to continue merge or rebase.
Finds whitespace errors in diffs, useful before completion.

scenario.question: After editing away conflict markers, what signals resolution?
scenario.explanation: Staging tells Git the conflict was resolved in that path.

lessons.tip: Resolve based on intended behavior, not merely deleting every line around a marker.
lessons.objective: Explain conflict marker and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Conflict marker: Temporary <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> lines identifying competing edits.
Conflict resolution: Human-selected merged content staged to continue merge or rebase.
git diff --check: Finds whitespace errors in diffs, useful before completion.
lessons.questStory: Mission 09: Your team needs you to apply resolve merge conflicts safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Automate with GitHub Actions
lessons.summary: A workflow YAML under .github/workflows declares events, jobs, and steps. Scope permissions to minimum necessary and pin trusted dependencies.

lab.prompt: List tracked GitHub Actions workflow files.
lab.hint: Use ls-files with the workflows folder.

concepts.definition: A YAML-defined automation triggered by repository events or manually.
A set of steps running in an environment, typically a runner.
Ephemeral workflow credential whose permissions should be limited.

scenario.question: A CI job only reads code and runs tests. Which permissions are appropriate?
scenario.explanation: Most test jobs only need repository contents: read.

lessons.tip: Never print secrets to logs or run untrusted PR code with privileged secrets.
lessons.objective: Explain workflow and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Workflow: A YAML-defined automation triggered by repository events or manually.
Job: A set of steps running in an environment, typically a runner.
GITHUB_TOKEN: Ephemeral workflow credential whose permissions should be limited.
lessons.questStory: Mission 10: Your team needs you to apply automate with github actions safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Images versus containers
lessons.summary: An image is the packaged, layered filesystem and config. A container is a running or stopped instance with isolated processes and a writable layer.

lab.prompt: List images available locally.
lab.hint: Use docker image followed by the list subcommand.

concepts.definition: An immutable-by-digest bundle of filesystem layers and execution configuration.
An instance of an image with process isolation and its own writable layer.
A service that stores and distributes OCI container images.

scenario.question: You want three running replicas of one application. What can you reuse?
scenario.explanation: Each replica can be a distinct container based on the same image.

lessons.tip: Tags such as latest are mutable; pin digests when reproducibility matters.
lessons.objective: Explain image and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Image: An immutable-by-digest bundle of filesystem layers and execution configuration.
Container: An instance of an image with process isolation and its own writable layer.
Registry: A service that stores and distributes OCI container images.
lessons.questStory: Mission 11: Your team needs you to apply images versus containers safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Run and inspect containers
lessons.summary: Start a container with docker run, list with docker ps, inspect metadata, and read logs. Published ports connect host traffic to a container port.

lab.prompt: List all containers, including stopped ones.
lab.hint: Use ps and include stopped containers.

concepts.definition: Creates and starts a new container from an image.
Shows both running and stopped containers.
Maps a host port to a container port using -p HOST:CONTAINER.

scenario.question: An app listens on port 80 in a container, reachable on localhost:8080. What run flag is needed?
scenario.explanation: The left side of -p is the host port, the right side the container port.

lessons.tip: Avoid publishing databases publicly unless there is a deliberate access policy.
lessons.objective: Explain docker run and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: docker run: Creates and starts a new container from an image.
docker ps -a: Shows both running and stopped containers.
Port publishing: Maps a host port to a container port using -p HOST:CONTAINER.
lessons.questStory: Mission 12: Your team needs you to apply run and inspect containers safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Container lifecycle and logs
lessons.summary: A container can be created, running, exited, or removed. Logs expose stdout/stderr; exec starts a process inside an already-running container.

lab.prompt: Read recent logs for a running container named web.
lab.hint: Use logs with the container name.

concepts.definition: Reads captured stdout and stderr from a container.
Starts an additional process within a running container.
Requests graceful shutdown, then may force stop after a timeout.

scenario.question: Your service exited immediately. What should you inspect first?
scenario.explanation: The process output commonly explains startup failures.

lessons.tip: Running an interactive shell does not fix a broken image; make corrections in source and rebuild.
lessons.objective: Explain docker logs and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: docker logs: Reads captured stdout and stderr from a container.
docker exec: Starts an additional process within a running container.
docker stop: Requests graceful shutdown, then may force stop after a timeout.
lessons.questStory: Mission 13: Your team needs you to apply container lifecycle and logs safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Volumes and persistence
lessons.summary: A container writable layer is removed when its container is removed. Named volumes store mutable application data outside that layer; bind mounts expose host paths.

lab.prompt: List volumes managed by Docker.
lab.hint: List volumes with the volume subcommand.

concepts.definition: Docker-managed persistent storage surviving container replacement until explicitly deleted.
Maps a chosen host directory or file into a container.
Container-specific filesystem changes that are not part of its image.

scenario.question: You replace a database container but must retain data. Best default?
scenario.explanation: A named volume outlives a single container instance.

lessons.tip: Beware docker compose down -v: the -v flag removes named volumes declared by the project.
lessons.objective: Explain named volume and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Named volume: Docker-managed persistent storage surviving container replacement until explicitly deleted.
Bind mount: Maps a chosen host directory or file into a container.
Writable layer: Container-specific filesystem changes that are not part of its image.
lessons.questStory: Mission 14: Your team needs you to apply volumes and persistence safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Networking and container DNS
lessons.summary: On a user-defined bridge network, containers can reach one another by name. Only publish ports that need host access, and avoid hardcoded container IPs.

lab.prompt: List Docker networks available on this host.
lab.hint: Use docker network and a listing subcommand.

concepts.definition: A common single-host Docker network mode providing container connectivity.
Resolution of container/service names to reachable network addresses.
A port published on a host interface and forwarded to a container port.

scenario.question: A web container connects to a db service in the same Compose network. Hostname should be:
scenario.explanation: Compose networks provide internal DNS resolving service names.

lessons.tip: Inside a container localhost refers to that container, not your database sibling.
lessons.objective: Explain bridge network and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Bridge network: A common single-host Docker network mode providing container connectivity.
Service discovery: Resolution of container/service names to reachable network addresses.
Host port: A port published on a host interface and forwarded to a container port.
lessons.questStory: Mission 15: Your team needs you to apply networking and container dns safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Write your first Dockerfile
lessons.summary: A Dockerfile describes image assembly. FROM picks a base, WORKDIR a working directory, COPY adds content, and CMD defines a default command.

lab.prompt: Build an image named academy with tag v1 from the current directory.
lab.hint: Use build -t and finish with a dot for the context.

concepts.definition: Sets a base image or build stage source.
Copies build-context files into the image filesystem.
Defines the default command or arguments when starting a container.

scenario.question: Which Dockerfile instruction copies local application source?
scenario.explanation: COPY adds source files from the build context.

lessons.tip: EXPOSE documents a port but does not publish it on the host.
lessons.objective: Explain from and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: FROM: Sets a base image or build stage source.
COPY: Copies build-context files into the image filesystem.
CMD: Defines the default command or arguments when starting a container.
lessons.questStory: Mission 16: Your team needs you to apply write your first dockerfile safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Image layers and caching
lessons.summary: Layer-aware builds reuse earlier work when inputs have not changed. Copy dependency manifests first, install dependencies, then copy frequently changed source files.

lab.prompt: Show the layer/build history for an image called academy:v1.
lab.hint: Use docker history and the image tag.

concepts.definition: Reuse of build steps when instructions and dependency inputs match.
Files sent or made available to an image build.
Patterns excluding unnecessary files from the build context.

scenario.question: Why copy package-lock.json before source code in a Node Dockerfile?
scenario.explanation: Dependencies often change less frequently than source files.

lessons.tip: Never COPY . before excluding .git, node_modules, and secret files.
lessons.objective: Explain layer cache and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Layer cache: Reuse of build steps when instructions and dependency inputs match.
Build context: Files sent or made available to an image build.
.dockerignore: Patterns excluding unnecessary files from the build context.
lessons.questStory: Mission 17: Your team needs you to apply image layers and caching safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Compose multi-service apps
lessons.summary: Compose defines services, networks, volumes, and configuration as versioned YAML. Services share default-network DNS by service name.

lab.prompt: Validate and render the effective Compose configuration.
lab.hint: Compose supports a config validation command.

concepts.definition: A named container specification under services in compose.yaml.
Expresses dependency ordering; readiness needs additional health conditions.
Parses and validates a Compose project and prints normalized configuration.

scenario.question: Your API needs Redis. Which hostname should it call inside Compose?
scenario.explanation: A service can resolve another service through Compose network DNS.

lessons.tip: depends_on alone does not guarantee the dependency is application-ready.
lessons.objective: Explain compose service and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Compose service: A named container specification under services in compose.yaml.
depends_on: Expresses dependency ordering; readiness needs additional health conditions.
docker compose config: Parses and validates a Compose project and prints normalized configuration.
lessons.questStory: Mission 18: Your team needs you to apply compose multi-service apps safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Small and hardened images
lessons.summary: Use multi-stage builds to avoid shipping compilers, pin trusted bases, run as non-root, drop unneeded capabilities, and never bake passwords into layers.

lab.prompt: Inspect metadata of the image academy:v1.
lab.hint: Use image inspect with the tagged image.

concepts.definition: Copies just the runtime artifacts out of earlier build stages.
Selects a non-root user for later build steps and runtime execution.
Content-addressed identifier that can pin a specific image version.

scenario.question: Which practice reduces runtime attack surface?
scenario.explanation: Removing build tools and dependencies reduces exposed runtime components.

lessons.tip: ARG and ENV do not provide safe permanent storage for build secrets.
lessons.objective: Explain multi-stage build and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Multi-stage build: Copies just the runtime artifacts out of earlier build stages.
USER instruction: Selects a non-root user for later build steps and runtime execution.
Image digest: Content-addressed identifier that can pin a specific image version.
lessons.questStory: Mission 19: Your team needs you to apply small and hardened images safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Health and observability
lessons.summary: Use health checks to detect when an application cannot serve requests, but distinguish process startup from readiness. Collect structured logs and explicit service metrics.

lab.prompt: Capture one snapshot of container CPU and memory usage.
lab.hint: Use stats without continuous streaming.

concepts.definition: A repeated probe used to mark container health independently of process existence.
Whether an application is currently ready to accept useful traffic.
Shows live CPU, memory, network, and I/O resource usage.

scenario.question: A process is running but cannot reach its database. What reveals the issue better?
scenario.explanation: Health checks should reflect application dependencies and service function.

lessons.tip: Avoid making liveness depend on every transient external dependency or restarts can amplify failures.
lessons.objective: Explain healthcheck and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Healthcheck: A repeated probe used to mark container health independently of process existence.
Readiness: Whether an application is currently ready to accept useful traffic.
docker stats: Shows live CPU, memory, network, and I/O resource usage.
lessons.questStory: Mission 20: Your team needs you to apply health and observability safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Cluster architecture
lessons.summary: A cluster has a control plane reconciling desired state and worker nodes running Pods. kubectl communicates with the API server according to your context.

lab.prompt: Display information about the configured Kubernetes control plane.
lab.hint: Use cluster-info.

concepts.definition: Components coordinating desired state, API access, and scheduling.
A machine providing resources for Pods.
Command-line client for talking to the Kubernetes API.

scenario.question: Which component accepts Kubernetes API requests?
scenario.explanation: The API server is the front door for cluster operations.

lessons.tip: Confirm kubectl context before applying or deleting resources.
lessons.objective: Explain control plane and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Control plane: Components coordinating desired state, API access, and scheduling.
Node: A machine providing resources for Pods.
kubectl: Command-line client for talking to the Kubernetes API.
lessons.questStory: Mission 21: Your team needs you to apply cluster architecture safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Pods and deployments
lessons.summary: A Pod is a scheduling unit containing one or more containers. A Deployment manages replicated, replaceable Pods via ReplicaSets and rollout strategies.

lab.prompt: List Deployments in the active namespace.
lab.hint: Ask kubectl to get deployments.

concepts.definition: Smallest deployable Kubernetes unit sharing networking and storage among containers.
Controller that maintains desired replicas and orchestrates rolling updates.
Controller maintaining a target number of matching Pods.

scenario.question: A Pod crashes and must be recreated automatically. What should own it?
scenario.explanation: A Deployment controller replaces unhealthy or missing Pods.

lessons.tip: Do not treat individual Pod names as stable endpoints.
lessons.objective: Explain pod and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Pod: Smallest deployable Kubernetes unit sharing networking and storage among containers.
Deployment: Controller that maintains desired replicas and orchestrates rolling updates.
ReplicaSet: Controller maintaining a target number of matching Pods.
lessons.questStory: Mission 22: Your team needs you to apply pods and deployments safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Services and networking
lessons.summary: Pods are ephemeral; a Service exposes a stable virtual address and selects backing Pods by labels. Ingress and Gateway APIs manage incoming HTTP traffic patterns.

lab.prompt: List cluster Services in your active namespace.
lab.hint: Use get services.

concepts.definition: Stable abstraction for addressing a selected set of Pods.
The default Service type, reachable within the cluster network.
API resource describing HTTP(S) ingress rules when an ingress controller is installed.

scenario.question: Your frontend must reach replaceable backend Pods. Use:
scenario.explanation: The Service remains a stable endpoint as Pods come and go.

lessons.tip: A Service selector must match target Pod labels, or it will have no endpoints.
lessons.objective: Explain service and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: Service: Stable abstraction for addressing a selected set of Pods.
ClusterIP: The default Service type, reachable within the cluster network.
Ingress: API resource describing HTTP(S) ingress rules when an ingress controller is installed.
lessons.questStory: Mission 23: Your team needs you to apply services and networking safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Configuration, secrets, storage
lessons.summary: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration; Secrets store sensitive bytes but need proper RBAC and encryption at rest. PVCs request durable volume storage.

lab.prompt: List ConfigMaps in the active namespace.
lab.hint: Use get configmaps.

concepts.definition: API object providing non-confidential app configuration.
API object for sensitive values; base64 encoding alone is not encryption.
Request for storage, commonly provisioned by a StorageClass.

scenario.question: A database password must be injected into a Pod. Better primitive?
options: Pod annotation in a public repo
scenario.explanation: Kubernetes Secret is built for sensitive config but still requires security controls.

lessons.tip: Never commit raw kubeconfig or unencrypted secrets to a public repository.
lessons.objective: Explain configmap and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: ConfigMap: API object providing non-confidential app configuration.
Secret: API object for sensitive values; base64 encoding alone is not encryption.
PersistentVolumeClaim: Request for storage, commonly provisioned by a StorageClass.
lessons.questStory: Mission 24: Your team needs you to apply configuration, secrets, storage safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Debugging and scaling
lessons.summary: Inspect describe/events/logs before guessing. Scale Deployments deliberately and use resource requests, limits, and autoscaling when load warrants it.

lab.prompt: List Pods with extended scheduling and IP information.
lab.hint: Include -o wide when getting pods.

concepts.definition: Provides detailed object state and related events for diagnosis.
Amount of CPU or memory used by the scheduler for placement.
Controller adjusting replica count based on configured metrics.

scenario.question: A Pod sits in Pending state. Which first action is useful?
scenario.explanation: Events often explain failed scheduling and unbound volumes.

lessons.tip: Autoscaling cannot compensate for an application that is fundamentally unhealthy.
lessons.objective: Explain kubectl describe and apply it in a practical workflow.
takeaways: kubectl describe: Provides detailed object state and related events for diagnosis.
Resource request: Amount of CPU or memory used by the scheduler for placement.
HorizontalPodAutoscaler: Controller adjusting replica count based on configured metrics.
lessons.questStory: Mission 25: Your team needs you to apply debugging and scaling safely. Read the intel, validate your choice, and enter the required command in the simulated terminal.

lessons.title: Cloud models and shared responsibility
lessons.summary: Cloud services offer on-demand resources. You still own identity, data classification, application logic, and many configuration choices even when a provider operates hardware.

lab.prompt: Check the AWS CLI version in a local sandbox (no credentials needed).

concepts.definition: Infrastructure as a Service: rented compute, network, and storage primitives.
